questions.q: Define "estimator variables" and "system variables" in eyewitness memory research, giving one Indian-context example of each.
questions.a: Estimator variables are uncontrolled event factors affecting encoding (e.g., poor street lighting at a Mumbai local station during monsoon evening). System variables are controllable justice-system factors affecting retrieval (e.g., Delhi Police using simultaneous vs. sequential photo lineup procedure). A wrong answer confusing these categories reveals the student cannot distinguish between encoding-stage and retrieval-stage influences — a fundamental error in applying Wells's (1978) framework to real cases.

questions.q: Explain why the "weapon focus effect" reduces eyewitness accuracy for perpetrator identification, using the concept of attentional narrowing and Levels of Processing theory.
questions.a: Weapon focus narrows attention to the threatening object (gun/knife) at the expense of peripheral details like the perpetrator's face. This forces shallow structural/phonetic processing (Level 1-2) of facial features instead of deep semantic encoding (Level 3), per Craik & Lockhart. A wrong answer attributing this only to "stress" without linking to attentional allocation and depth-of-processing reveals the student treats stress as a unitary cause rather than analyzing its cognitive mechanism.

questions.q: A witness views a 30-second robbery at 9 PM under a flickering sodium-vapor lamp (estimator: poor lighting). Police conduct a simultaneous lineup 48 hours later where the suspect is the only one wearing a red hoodie matching the witness's description (system: biased lineup). Apply the "misinformation effect" and "source monitoring error" to predict how the witness's confidence-accuracy relationship will be distorted.
questions.a: Step 1: Poor lighting during encoding creates weak, fragmentary memory trace. Step 2: Biased lineup (red hoodie only on suspect) acts as post-event suggestion — witness infers "police think it's this person." Step 3: During retrieval, witness confuses familiarity from lineup exposure with original memory (source monitoring error). Step 4: High confidence emerges from fluency of recognition, not accuracy — confidence-accuracy correlation drops toward zero. Wrong answers ignoring the 48-hour delay's role in memory decay reveal failure to integrate Ebbinghaus forgetting curve with retrieval contamination.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the "cross-race effect" (own-race bias) and "weapon focus effect" as estimator variables. Which poses a greater threat to identification accuracy in a diverse Indian metro city context? Justify using cognitive mechanisms.
questions.a: Cross-race effect stems from differential expertise: perceptual systems optimize for frequently encountered facial configurations (own-race), leading to configural vs. feature-based processing differences. Weapon focus stems from evolutionary attentional capture by threat. In diverse Indian metros (Delhi/Mumbai), cross-race effect is less pronounced due to daily exposure to varied phenotypes, whereas weapon focus operates universally. Greater threat: weapon focus — it directly degrades encoding of the only identifying feature (face) regardless of witness-perpetrator racial match. Wrong answers claiming cross-race effect dominates reveal misunderstanding of perceptual expertise plasticity in multicultural environments.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "Eyewitness confidence is a reliable indicator of identification accuracy because confident witnesses have clearer memories." Use Loftus's post-event information research and the confidence-malleability hypothesis.
questions.a: The statement is invalid. Loftus (1979) showed post-event misinformation (e.g., "Did you see the broken headlight?" vs. "a broken headlight?") inflates confidence without improving accuracy. Confidence-malleability hypothesis: confidence is influenced by non-diagnostic factors (feedback, repeated questioning, lineup format) after the fact. In Indian courts, Section 118 Evidence Act treats confident testimony as credible — a dangerous policy given confidence-accuracy correlation of only r = 0.25-0.30. Wrong answers citing "confidence means strong encoding" confuse retrieval fluency with storage strength, ignoring reconstructive nature of memory.

questions.q: Design a 5-step police lineup protocol for a Bengaluru theft case that minimizes system-variable contamination, incorporating sequential presentation, blind administration, confidence statements, filler selection criteria, and documentation. Explain how each step addresses a specific memory distortion mechanism.
questions.a: Step 1: Blind administrator (doesn't know suspect) prevents unconscious cuing → reduces demand characteristics. Step 2: Sequential presentation (one photo at a time) forces absolute judgment vs. relative judgment in simultaneous lineups → reduces false identifications by 22% (Steblay et al., 2001). Step 3: Pre-lineup instruction "perpetrator may not be present" → lowers criterion shift from "choose best match" to "recognize or reject." Step 4: Fillers match witness description (not suspect) → prevents suspect standing out (biased lineup). Step 5: Immediate confidence statement (0-100%) documented before feedback → preserves pre-contamination confidence-accuracy diagnostic value. Poor answers listing generic "fair procedures" without linking each step to a specific cognitive mechanism (relative judgment, criterion shift, source monitoring) reveal superficial procedural knowledge without theoretical grounding.

What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Eyewitness memory?
questions.a: Students believe eyewitness memory works like a video camera — if you "saw it," the memory is stored intact and retrieval simply plays it back.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to evaluate a simulated eyewitness scenario by identifying at least three estimator and two system variables affecting recall accuracy, explain the misinformation effect mechanism using Loftus's research, and distinguish between reproductive and reconstructive memory errors in a written response of 150-200 words.
